Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir hold that creation and restoration apply to all creatures. On the names al-Ghafur and al-Wadud, Ibn 'Abbas explains the latter as the beloved, Mujahid as the one who loves His allies, and Ibn Zayd as the merciful; al-Mawardi adds that al-Ghafur covers faults and pardons sins, and that al-Wadud may also mean one without offspring. As for "Lord of the Glorious Throne", the reading with a kasra, attributed to Hamza and al-Kisa'i, makes "glorious" describe the Throne, while the reading with a damma makes it describe God; al-Tabari regards both readings as correct, and Ibn Kathir considers both sound. The intensive form "fa''al" is explained by al-Zamakhshari as indicating the great abundance of what He wills and does, and al-Razi draws from it arguments in the debate about the creation of human acts.

The verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ with a question: has the account of the hosts reached you? The commentators explain that the hosts are the armies gathered against the messengers through harm. Pharaoh is named as representing his people and followers, and Thamud is added. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi read the passage as consolation for the Prophet and a warning to the polytheists of Mecca, who are in persistent denial as their predecessors were. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan say the question serves to draw attention and to magnify the matter. Ibn Ashur says the term refers to nations gathered to resist the messengers, and that the question aims to make the account seem grave. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir explain why these two peoples are mentioned: Thamud was well known in Arabia, and Pharaoh was famous among the People of the Book and the pre-Islamic Arabs. Al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi connect the passage to God's power, which surrounds the disbelievers and preserves the Quran in a guarded tablet. Most commentators do not choose among the differing interpretations of the words.

This verse tells us that God addressed His Prophet ﷺ about 'the story of the armies', meaning the hosts that rose against God's messengers to harm them, and then names them: 'Pharaoh and Thamud'. Pharaoh is in apposition to 'the armies', either as 'the armies of Pharaoh' or as Pharaoh together with his people, whom he led. The purpose is to console the Prophet ﷺ and to warn his people that their fate will resemble theirs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya link the passage to the phrase 'indeed the seizure of your Lord is severe', so that the mention of Pharaoh and Thamud serves as proof of the severity of God's punishment of wrongdoers. Al-Razi argues that the relationship between believers and disbelievers follows the same pattern in every age. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the turn 'but those who disbelieve' shows that the denial of the Prophet's own people is worse than that of earlier nations, since they witnessed the ruin of those before them and took no lesson. The commentators recall that Thamud lived in Arabia and their story was known there, while Pharaoh's story was famous among the People of the Book and among the Arabs of the pre-Islamic era. Most agree on the general meaning and differ mainly over the grammar and how the passage connects to what precedes it. God knows best.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the mention of Pharaoh, Thamud and the armies, and states that the disbelievers among the Prophet's contemporaries persist in denial without taking lesson from the fate of earlier peoples; denial encompasses them as a container encompasses what it holds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify them as the Quraysh, and note that God surrounds them with His knowledge and power so that they cannot escape Him. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud read the particle « bal » as a shift to a graver case: their guilt exceeds that of those peoples, since they witnessed the traces of destruction and still did not heed them. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the object of the denial is implied by context, namely the Prophet, the revelation and the resurrection. Al-Shinqiti compares this with the parallel in Surat al-Inshiqaq, where the wording is « yukadhdhibun », and attributes the difference to the rhyme of the verses. Ibn 'Uthaymin argues that « alladhina kafaru » covers anyone who disbelieves in the Prophet, whether polytheist, Jew or Christian. All agree that the verse consoles the Prophet and warns his opponents, before the following verses exalt the Qur'an preserved in the Guarded Tablet.

The commentators explain that this verse comes after the mention of Pharaoh, Thamud and other peoples who denied their messengers. It affirms that the contemporaries of the Prophet ﷺ persist in denial and obstinacy, and that God encompasses them with His knowledge and power, so they cannot escape Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud understand this encompassing as God knowing their deeds, recompensing them, and being able to punish them, and they take it as a warning. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi read it as an image: they are like someone surrounded from behind who finds no way of escape, and al-Razi adds that it may mean their destruction is near. Ibn 'Ashur holds that it depicts a punishment that overtakes the heedless, not merely God's knowledge. Ibn al-Qayyim notes how strange it is to deny the One who holds them. The verse then turns to rebut their accusations: al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya say the Quran is glorious and unharmed by this denial, since God guards it. On the Preserved Tablet, the commentators agree it is safe from alteration and from the devils. They differ on its nature: according to Anas it is on Israfil's forehead, according to Muqatil it is to the right of the Throne, and according to Ibn 'Abbas it is of white pearl. The readers differ too: Nafi' reads 'mahfuzun' in the nominative, describing the Quran, while most read it in the genitive, describing the Tablet. Al-Tabari considers both readings valid. No legal ruling is drawn from this verse.

The commentators explain that this verse answers those among the Quraysh who called the Qur'an poetry, rhymed prose, soothsaying or magic. God states that the matter is not as they claim: it is a noble and glorious Qur'an, exalted in its composition, meaning and blessing. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir agree that "majid" means noble and great, and the commentators stress that this is a speech beyond any human words. The verse belongs to a passage that consoles the Prophet ﷺ over his people's rejection, after the mention of the destruction of Pharaoh and Thamud, while the disbelievers persist in denial and God encompasses them with His power.

Scholars differ on the reading of "mahfuz" and on the nature of the Preserved Tablet. Al-Tabari holds that both readings are sound: either the Tablet is protected from any addition or omission, or the Qur'an is protected from alteration, as Nafi and those who read it in the nominative maintain. As for the Tablet, Mujahid and al-Tabari identify it with the Mother of the Book, Muqatil places it to the right of the Throne, and Anas, quoted by al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, locates it on the forehead of Israfil. Al-Zamakhshari describes it as being above the seventh heaven. Several accounts describing its form, cited by al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, are regarded as weak in their chains of transmission.

Other readings, such as reading "Qur'an of a glorious Lord" as a construct, are reported by al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, though none of them uses this to settle the meaning.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Qur'an as written on a preserved tablet, meaning protected from any addition, omission or corruption, and beyond the reach of the devils. On the general meaning, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the verse answers those who called the Qur'an poetry or soothsaying: it is glorious and noble, and its preservation is guaranteed. They also agree that 'preserved' means safeguarded against alteration and distortion. There is a difference in recitation: most readers read 'mahfuzin' in the genitive, describing the tablet, while Nafi' and Ibn Muhaysin read 'mahfuzun' in the nominative, describing the Qur'an. Al-Tabari considers both readings correct and equivalent in meaning. On the nature of the tablet, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it to be the Mother of the Book with God, where everything is recorded. Ibn 'Abbas describes it as a white pearl, as long as the distance between heaven and earth, joined to the Throne. Anas and Mujahid place it on the forehead of Israfil, Muqatil at the right of the Throne, and al-Hasan sees it as something that appears to the angels so that they may read it. Al-Zamakhshari locates it above the seventh heaven, in the air. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that these reports rest on weak chains of transmission. Ibn 'Ashur concludes that the most reliable point is that it is a sacred record whose precise nature remains unknown.
